summary.text: Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a liquid or a gas.
It is named after Robert Brown, who in 1827 watched pollen grains in water under a microscope and saw them make a continuous, jittery motion.
Einstein's 1905 explanation, with water molecules pushing the particles, served as convincing evidence that atoms and molecules exist, and Jean Perrin verified it in 1908.

facts.label: First described
facts.value: Robert Brown, 1827, using pollen in water

facts.label: Experimental proof
facts.value: Jean Perrin verified Einstein's explanation in 1908

facts.label: Rigorous mathematics
facts.value: Norbert Wiener gave the first complete analysis in 1923

facts.label: Early finance model
facts.value: Louis Bachelier modeled it in his 1900 thesis on speculation

facts.label: Not alive
facts.value: Glass and rock dust jitter too

items.prompt: A scientist sees pollen grains jitter in still water. He repeats the test with glass dust and rock dust, and they jitter as well. What does this tell him?

options.label: The jitter only happens with powdered stone
The jitter comes from the grains being alive
The motion is not caused by anything living
The microscope is making the grains shake

items.explain: Brown found the same motion in inorganic matter, so he could rule out that it was life-related.

items.prompt: A speck floats in a glass of still water and wanders unpredictably. What best explains the wandering?

options.label: Water molecules hit it harder on one side at different moments
The speck pushes itself through the water in random directions
The water steadily flows in one direction and carries it along
Each water molecule hits it from the same side every time

items.explain: The direction of the molecular bombardment keeps changing, so the particle is hit more on one side than another at different times.

items.prompt: In 1905 many scientists still argued over whether atoms were real. Why did explaining a visible jiggle help settle that?

options.label: Atoms were seen directly through the microscope that year
The jiggle was shown to come from the particle's own heat
The pollen turned out to be made of single atoms
A jiggle explained by molecule impacts and then tested pointed to unseen molecules

items.explain: Einstein explained the motion as impacts of individual molecules, and experiments verified it, which served as convincing evidence that atoms and molecules exist.

items.prompt: Why do scientists describe this motion with probability models rather than tracking every molecule involved?

options.label: Molecules in a liquid never obey any physical laws
The many-body interactions cannot be solved by modeling every molecule
Nobody has ever measured the position of a single particle
A single formula already predicts every individual collision

items.explain: The many-body interactions behind the pattern cannot be solved by a model accounting for every molecule, so only probabilistic models applied to molecular populations are used.

items.prompt: A pollen grain floats in a cup of water kept at one steady temperature. How does the fluid around it behave overall?

options.label: It has no preferred direction of flow
It slowly pushes everything toward the cup's edge
It spins steadily in one direction
It flows from the warm side toward the cool side

items.explain: The pattern describes a fluid at thermal equilibrium at a given temperature, and in such a fluid there is no preferential direction of flow.

items.prompt: A mathematician writes about Brownian motion in a research paper. What is she most likely referring to?

options.label: Only the motion of pollen seen in water
A particle that always drifts in one direction
A process describing the movement of stock prices only
The Wiener process, its traditional mathematical formulation

items.explain: The traditional mathematical formulation of Brownian motion is the Wiener process, which is often itself called Brownian motion, even in mathematical sources.
